messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 29
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Jeweler
  trauma_type: Relief worker in war zone
  pcl5: 70

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Somatic (Heart Racing): Own heart racing or pounding, Auditory (Children Crying): Kids crying, Tactile (Unexpected Touch): Being touched unprepared
  Maladaptive Strategies: Downward Comparison: I remind myself it could have been worse, Positive Reframing: I force myself to think only positive thoughts, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment, Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things

Vignette:
Daniel had been working as a relief volunteer in a war zone for several months when the incident that still organized his days occurred. At 29, he had signed up believing he could help in practical ways, and for a while his work had been the kind that left little room for reflection: distributing supplies, moving through damaged streets, keeping notes, trying to stay useful. One afternoon, while he was in a crowded area near a distribution point, a sudden burst of chaos swept through the street. He had been close enough to hear children crying in the confusion, a sound that cut through everything else and fixed itself in his mind. In the same moment, he became acutely aware of his own heart pounding hard in his chest, a physical sensation he now remembers with particular dread because it seemed to announce that something terrible was happening even before he could fully understand it. He also remembers being grabbed unexpectedly as people pushed past him, the kind of unprepared touch that made him jolt with a force he still cannot explain to himself. He got out, but the event remained vivid in a way that ordinary life never has. When he tries to describe it now, he says it feels more real than other memories, as if the scene has sharper edges and brighter sound than anything else he has lived through.

In the weeks that followed, Daniel found that the memory could seize him without warning. Something in his surroundings — a child’s cry in a store, a sudden thump in the building next to his apartment, someone brushing past him in a narrow aisle — could bring the whole scene back at full force before he had time to prepare. At times the memory arrived with no clear picture at all, but with the same heavy emotional intensity that he had felt in the war zone, leaving him tense, exposed, and briefly unable to focus on where he was. He became preoccupied with signs of danger wherever he went. In his work as a jeweler, he now notices potential weapons and dangerous objects almost automatically, scanning the counter, the shop floor, and even customers’ hands for anything that could be used against him. He positions himself with his back against a wall whenever possible so that he can see the room, and if he cannot do that he feels uneasy enough that it is difficult to concentrate on shaping metal or setting stones. He has come to distrust reassurance, saying that even when people tell him he is safe, he cannot really believe them. The words may be kind, but they do not reach the part of him that remains on alert.

This has changed his everyday life in concrete ways. In the jewelry shop, Daniel is outwardly steady and competent, but he is constantly checking the entrance, the mirrors, and the positions of customers who enter while he is bent over a workbench. The small, sharp tools around him, once ordinary parts of his trade, now draw his attention in a way that feels unavoidable. He has learned to take breaks when his chest starts to pound, though the sensation itself can be enough to pull him back into the memory. He avoids crowded places when he can, not by naming it as avoidance, but by organizing his life so that he has less contact with situations in which someone might touch him without warning or where children’s crying might catch him off guard. Friends have noticed that he seems distant and hard to reassure, and he has begun turning down invitations because being in unfamiliar rooms leaves him too busy looking for exits, walls, and objects that might be used as weapons.

Daniel has tried to manage the experience by telling himself it could have been worse, reminding himself that others did not get out at all, and forcing himself to think positively when the memories break through. He uses these thoughts as if they could hold the feelings in place, but they rarely last. More often, they sit alongside a persistent sense that the world is not safe in the way other people seem to believe. He is single and lives alone, and he has noticed that even at home he chooses seats with a clear view of the door and keeps himself near walls rather than in the middle of a room. He finally sought help after realizing how much of his day was arranged around watching for danger, and after a recent moment in the shop when a child cried outside the front window and his heart began racing so hard that he had to step away from a customer. He says he wants to keep working without feeling as though he is back in that street every time his chest pounds or someone reaches toward him, but what he fears most is that he will never again be able to trust safety when it is offered to him.
